sources.cite: NASEMSO National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, Version 3.0 (rev. March 2022): Hypoglycemia
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in full text (the copy Iowa HHS hosts, https://hhs.iowa.gov/media/198/download; NASEMSO refused the PDF on 2026-11-09). Still the current version (no Version 4 found 2026-11-11). Treat at 60 mg/dL or less. Conscious with a patent airway: oral glucose 25 g. Unconscious or unable to protect the airway: dextrose IV in incremental doses until mental status improves or the field maximum is reached (D10 preferred; adult maximum 25 g, 250 mL of D10); glucagon 1 mg IM/IN when IV access cannot be established. Reassess vital signs and mental status; repeat the glucose if mental status has not returned to normal. Release without transport only if all hold: repeat glucose > 80, insulin or metformin without a long-acting sulfonylurea, normal mental status, can promptly eat a meal, refuses and the clinicians agree transport is not indicated, a reliable adult will stay, no major comorbid symptoms, a clear cause. D10 is as effective and safer than stronger concentrations; avoid overshoot hyperglycemia.

sources.cite: NHTSA. National EMS Scope of Practice Model 2019 (DOT HS 812 666), with Change Notices 1.0 and 2.0 (2021)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-11 in a text extraction of the Louisiana copy (the extractor did not keep every table column, so placement was checked against the course's own reading of 2026-11-09 in ems-sources.ts). EMR: CPR and AED, tourniquet and wound packing, naloxone, oral airway, BVM, oxygen; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, epinephrine auto-injector, aspirin, oral glucose, CPAP, 12-lead acquisition (not interpretation), transport. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways and a limited list of IV and IM medications including dextrose and glucagon. Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, intubation and the wider formulary. No newer model was found 2026-11-11 (EMS.gov's page was unavailable; the only other 'update' found is the 2017 change notice adding tourniquets, wound packing and naloxone to EMR and EMT).

brief.situation: 12:40. You are the AEMT on an ambulance with an EMT partner, called to a warehouse break room. Mr. Duval, 54, about 85 kg, is slumped in a chair, sweaty and snoring; a coworker found him like this a few minutes ago.
handover: Coworker: "He's diabetic, insulin. He had his lunch shot at noon, then got called onto the loading dock. There's a beer can on the table, but that's from the last shift, I think."

Within AEMT scope: airway adjuncts and supraglottic airways, waveform capnography, IV and IO access, IV dextrose (D10 carried), IM glucagon, IV or IN naloxone, oral glucose for a patient who can swallow.
The nearest emergency department is 15 minutes away.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
His glucose keeps falling while his lunch insulin acts. IV access and each dose take time; reassess after each one.
Partway through you are asked to explain your reasoning in writing. The case ends at the hospital (or when you leave him), then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. With rapid-acting insulin near its peak and no food, glucose falls about 0.8 mg/dL per minute. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. He seizes if glucose reaches 28 mg/dL in this case; severe hypoglycemia causes seizures, without a fixed threshold. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Each gram of IV dextrose raises this 85 kg man's glucose by about 4.5 mg/dL in the minutes after it runs in. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
A 100 mL (10 g) D10 dose runs in about 3 minutes through an 18-gauge line.

FLAG: stands in for a number no guideline gives. Glucagon 1 mg IM acts like about 10 g of dextrose spread over about 10 minutes. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

effects.log: Responds to pain with moaning, eyes open to pain (GCS 8). Snoring, gurgling. RR 12. Skin cold and drenched in sweat. Pupils midsize and reactive. No sign of injury; insulin pen in his shirt pocket.
Jaw thrust, a little saliva suctioned, a lubricated nasal airway in: quiet, clear breathing.
Pulse oximeter and nasal capnography on.

naloxone.label: Naloxone 0.4 mg IN, in case it's an overdose

effects.log: No change. His breathing rate was normal and his pupils were not pinpoint: nothing pointed to opioids.

oralGlucose.label: Oral glucose gel between his cheek and gum

then.log: He gurgles and coughs the gel into his airway: he cannot swallow or protect his airway.

refusal.title: "I'm fine, I just skipped lunch"
refusal.context: Mr. Duval is awake and oriented, glucose {gluLast} mg/dL. He took his rapid-acting lunch insulin at noon and has eaten nothing; he lives alone and his coworkers are going back to work. He wants to go back to his shift.

choices.label: Check his capacity, explain that his insulin is still acting and the sugar can drop again, offer transport, and call medical control if he still refuses

effects.log: He listens: "Alright, if it could happen again while I'm alone... I'll go."

choices.feedback: Release without transport needs every NASEMSO condition; here no reliable adult will stay and his insulin is still acting.

choices.label: He's awake and his sugar is up: have him eat a sandwich and sign a refusal

effects.log: He signs, eats half a sandwich and goes back to the dock.

choices.feedback: Not every release condition holds: he will be alone, and his lunch insulin is still acting.

effects.log: He opens his eyes and asks what happened.
He starts to twitch; his eyes flicker.

why.question: Why was this hypoglycemia and not alcohol or an overdose, and how did you decide how much dextrose to give?

parts.label: Analyzing the cues
parts.criteria: Insulin-dependent diabetic who took insulin and missed his meal, cold sweaty skin, tachycardia, normal breathing rate and pupils: hypoglycemia first; check glucose in any altered mental status; the beer can and naloxone are distractors (no opioid signs). Airway first: snoring needs a jaw thrust and an adjunct, and no oral glucose for a patient who cannot swallow.
parts.modelAnswer: He's an insulin user who took his lunch dose and didn't eat, and he's cold, sweaty and tachycardic with a normal breathing rate and normal pupils. That fits hypoglycemia, not opioids; the old beer can doesn't explain it. Open the airway first, check the glucose, and nothing by mouth while he can't swallow.

parts.label: Titrating and evaluating
parts.criteria: D10 IV in increments (10 g), reassess mental status and glucose after each, repeat until mental status improves, up to 25 g; glucagon IM only without IV access; avoid overshoot; transport because his insulin is still acting and he will be alone.
parts.modelAnswer: Give D10 in 10 g steps, recheck his mental status and glucose after each, and repeat until he is awake, staying within 25 g and avoiding overshoot. If there were no IV, glucagon 1 mg IM. Once awake, he still needs transport: his insulin is still working and nobody will stay with him.

noProgress.rationale: He reaches the hospital safely but still not fully awake: treatment was slow or too little. This case calls it recovered.

The snoring airway was never opened.

Glucagon only, though an IV was possible: slower.

reasoningCriteria.label: Written reasoning: the cues and the titration

expertPath.text: GCS 8, snoring, cold and sweaty, insulin pen in his pocket. Jaw thrust, suction, nasal airway; oxygen; monitor with capnography. Glucose: 34 mg/dL.
IV 18 gauge. Nothing by mouth. D10 100 mL (10 g).
Reassess: GCS rising, glucose about 60. Another 10 g. No naloxone: no opioid signs.
Awake, glucose about 100. He wants to stay: capacity, risks (insulin still acting, alone), offer transport; he agrees. Load, report, reassess en route.

seizure.headline: He seized
seizure.body: Glucose kept falling while his insulin acted. Look at when the glucose was checked, when the IV went in, and whether time went to naloxone or waiting.

aspiration.headline: Glucose into the airway
aspiration.body: Oral glucose is only for a patient who can swallow and protect the airway. With GCS 8 the route is IV dextrose (or IM glucagon without an IV).

releasedUnsafe.headline: Released alone
releasedUnsafe.body: NASEMSO lists every condition for release after hypoglycemia; a reliable adult staying and a clear plan are among them. His lunch insulin was still acting.

awakeAtEd.headline: Awake, safely transported
awakeAtEd.body: Airway first, glucose fast, D10 in steps with rechecks, cues followed, and a respectful conversation about why he should come. The expert path.

arrivedGaps.headline: Arrived, with gaps
arrivedGaps.body: Check the airway, the time to the first glucose and dextrose, whether you titrated and rechecked, overshoot, and how the decision to transport was made.

scoring.modelReasoning: An insulin user who took his dose and missed a meal, now cold, sweaty, tachycardic and snoring with normal pupils and breathing rate, is hypoglycemic until proven otherwise; the beer can is a distractor and there are no opioid signs. Airway first: jaw thrust, suction, a nasal airway, oxygen and capnography. Check glucose at once (34 mg/dL). He cannot swallow, so no oral glucose: IV access and D10 in 10 g steps, reassessing mental status and glucose after each, up to 25 g; glucagon 1 mg IM only if an IV cannot be placed. Avoid overshoot. Once awake he still needs transport: his insulin is still acting and he will be alone, so check capacity, explain the risk and offer transport, involving medical control if he refuses.

d10.ask: While the IV goes in: why D10 rather than D50?

choices.label: As effective, less tissue damage if it leaks, less overshoot

d10.explain: NASEMSO: D10 is as effective and safer; D50 can damage tissue if it extravasates and overshoots glucose.
